title: Ticketmaster
prompt: Design a ticketing system like Ticketmaster. Users browse events, see available seats, hold a seat while paying, and complete purchase. The system must handle flash-sale spikes (e.g. a Taylor Swift on-sale) without overselling. Target 100M users globally and peak loads of 1M concurrent buyers per popular event.

stages.title: Functional Requirements
stages.questionPrompt: What are the core functional requirements?
stages.howToAnswer: Browse, view seats, reserve, purchase. Skip account features.

must: Users can see available seats for an event
Users can reserve / hold a seat
Users can purchase a held seat
should: Hold expires automatically if not purchased
avoid: Mixing search and recommendations into the core

stages.sampleAnswer:
1. Users can browse events.
2. Users can see which seats are available for a given event.
3. Users can reserve (hold) a specific seat.
4. Users can complete payment within the hold window to purchase it.
hints: Walk through what a buyer actually does, in order. Browse → see seats → pick one → pay.
Reserve and purchase are different actions — why? What changes between them?
Skip the artist-onboarding side and recommendation features — they're separate products.

stages.title: Non-Functional Requirements
stages.howToAnswer: The headline NFR here is no-double-booking — strong consistency on seat state. Then talk scale (peak concurrent buyers) and availability.

must: No double-booking — strong consistency on seat reservation
should: Fairness during flash sales (queue, no front-running)
avoid: Saying 'eventual consistency is fine' for seat state

stages.sampleAnswer:
- Strong consistency: a seat can only be held by one user at a time. No double-bookings, ever.
- Scale: 1M concurrent buyers on a popular sale. Browsing reads must remain <200ms.
- Hold semantics: 10-min TTL. Auto-released on expiry.
- Fairness: a virtual waiting queue during high-demand sales.
- Availability: 99.95% during sales.
hints: What's the one thing that can never happen on this system? That's the headline NFR.
Latency, scale, availability — every NFR needs a number. The flash-sale spike is where most candidates undersize.
How long should a hold last? What happens when the user walks away during checkout?

stages.title: Core Entities
stages.howToAnswer: List the nouns. Be precise about what's a Seat vs SeatHold vs Ticket.
stages.sampleAnswer:
- Event: name, datetime, venue.
- Venue: contains a SeatMap (rows × columns, sections).
- Seat: belongs to a SeatMap. State per Event: AVAILABLE / HELD / SOLD.
- SeatHold: (seatId, eventId, userId, expiresAt). Transient.
- Booking: persistent record of a sold seat (seatId, eventId, userId, paymentId).
hints: Be precise: what's a Seat vs a Ticket vs a Hold? They have different lifecycles.
A SeatHold is transient; a Booking is permanent. Why is that distinction worth making at this level?

stages.title: API
stages.howToAnswer: Browse, get seats with state, reserve atomically, purchase. Reservation is the interesting one.

must: Endpoint to get seat availability for an event
Endpoint to reserve a seat (must be atomic)
Endpoint to confirm purchase against a hold
avoid: GET /seats returning the entire venue every poll (use sparse delta)
Reserve endpoint that doesn't return a hold token

hints: Listing is easy. The reserve endpoint is the one to think hardest about — what does it need to return?
What happens if two of three requested seats are available and one isn't? All-or-nothing or partial?
Use idempotency keys on the writes — why? What does the client do on a network blip?

stages.title: High-Level Design
stages.questionPrompt: Sketch the architecture. The hot path is reserve.
stages.howToAnswer: API → reservation service → DB with row-level locking OR Redis with a Lua script. Reads can be served from a cache. Mention fan-out for the queue during spikes.

must: An atomic reserve mechanism (DB transaction with row lock OR Redis SETNX/Lua)
Separation of read path (cached availability) and write path (reservation)
should: CDN / cache for static event metadata
Async pipeline for purchase confirmation (payment is slow)
avoid: 'Just lock the seat row in Postgres' without addressing connection-pool exhaustion at 1M concurrent
Optimistic concurrency on the seat row alone (livelock under contention)

stages.sampleAnswer:
Reads (browsing, seat availability): served from Redis with the seat-state map per event. Background job rebuilds from authoritative DB on changes. CDN in front for /events.

Writes (reserve): client POSTs to Reservation Service. Service runs a Redis Lua script that atomically checks each seat is AVAILABLE, marks them HELD with the holdId, and sets a 10-min TTL on the hold key. If the script fails on any seat, the entire reserve fails atomically. Successful holds are also written-through to the authoritative Postgres for durability.

Expiration: Redis TTL fires → a sweeper picks up expired holds and flips the seat back to AVAILABLE in both Redis and Postgres.

Purchase: POST /holds/:id/purchase enqueues a payment job (idempotent). Worker calls payment provider, on success flips seat from HELD to SOLD and writes a Booking row.
hints: The read path (browsing, availability) and the write path (reserve) have very different consistency needs. Don't lump them together.
For the write path, name the atomic primitive. DB transactions, Redis Lua scripts, or unique constraints — pick one and explain why.
Holds expire. Where does the timer live, and what flips the seat back to available?

deepDives.title: Preventing double-booking
deepDives.questionPrompt: How do you guarantee that two users hitting reserve at the exact same instant can't both win the same seat?
deepDives.sampleAnswer: Use a Redis Lua script: KEYS = the seat keys, ARGV = holdId + TTL. The script reads each seat's status; if any is not AVAILABLE, it returns -1 and writes nothing — the whole reservation aborts. If all are AVAILABLE, it SETs them all to HELD:holdId with the TTL, in the same atomic step. Lua scripts on a single Redis primary are serialized, so two concurrent reserves can't both win. The hold is written through to Postgres asynchronously for durability — the source-of-truth for availability stays Redis during the sale.

must: Atomic check-and-set across all requested seats
Explain why concurrent reserves can't race
should: Failure path: what the loser sees
avoid: Per-seat optimistic CAS (livelock when 5 seats contended individually)

hints: If two requests arrive at the same instant, what data structure resolves the contention? Where does it live?
An atomic primitive across N seats is harder than across 1. What goes wrong with per-seat optimistic locking when 5 seats are contended individually?
Whatever mechanism you pick, the loser must learn it lost. What does the failure response look like to the client?

deepDives.title: Flash-sale spike (1M concurrent)
deepDives.questionPrompt: How does the system handle a Taylor Swift on-sale with 1M users hitting reserve simultaneously?
deepDives.sampleAnswer: Front the reservation API with a virtual waiting room. On sale start, all clients get a queue token; an admission service releases ~10× the seat count per minute into the live booking flow. Behind the wall, the reservation service is what we'd ordinarily build — it just sees a controlled trickle, not 1M RPS. Token gives a position estimate so the user has a stable progress signal. After admission, the user has a 10-min hold window, then their slot recycles. FIFO with jitter keeps fairness; tokens are signed JWTs so we don't keep server-side state per waiting user.

must: Admission control before the reserve hot path
avoid: Counting on 'just autoscale' for 1M concurrent reserves
A queue that requires server-side state per waiter

hints: 1M concurrent on the reserve hot path is unrealistic for any DB or cache. What's the real strategy?
Throttle at the front door, not the back. Where does the throttle live, and what does the user see?
How do you make it feel fair without storing per-waiter state on the server?

deepDives.title: Reliable hold expiration
deepDives.questionPrompt: A hold is supposed to release after 10 minutes if not purchased. How do you guarantee that doesn't get missed under load?
deepDives.sampleAnswer: Primary mechanism: Redis TTL on the hold key. A subscriber on keyspace expiration events flips the seat from HELD back to AVAILABLE atomically (Lua to avoid a race with a late purchase). Secondary safety net: a sweeper job runs every minute scanning expired holds in Postgres for any that the Redis path missed (e.g., during a Redis failover). Idempotency: the AVAILABLE flip is a no-op if the seat is already SOLD.

avoid: Cron-only with a long interval (visible double-bookable window)
Trusting a single in-memory timer on one host

hints: What's the minimum visible double-bookable window if your only timer is a cron every minute?
Combine a primary mechanism with a backup sweeper — why? What does each cover?
Watch the race between expiry and a late purchase landing at the same moment. How do you keep that idempotent?
